analysis.one_liner: Requires every voting machine to produce a paper record voters can verify, with mandatory hand-count audits.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 222 cosponsors — more than half the House — but was never given a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the 2002 Help America Vote Act to require every voting system to produce a voter-verified permanent paper record that voters could inspect before casting their ballot. It would make that paper record the official document for any recount or audit, and require the Election Assistance Commission to run random, unannounced hand counts of paper records in at least 2% of precincts in every state after each federal election. It also banned undisclosed software and wireless or internet connections in voting machines, required disclosure of source code, banned financial conflicts of interest at testing labs, gave individuals a way to file complaints with the Attorney General, and authorized $150 million to help states pay for the changes.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyday voters, especially in states using paperless electronic voting machines. The bill guaranteed each voter a chance to check a paper record of their vote before it was cast, made paper the official record in recounts, and required random hand-count audits to catch machine errors or tampering. It also created a complaint process for voters who saw election rules violated, and gave voters with disabilities and non-English speakers accessible ways to verify their ballots.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters, election-integrity advocates, disabled and non-English voters

how_it_helps.text: Every voting system would have to produce a voter-verified paper record the voter can inspect and correct before the vote is cast, and the paper record becomes the true and official record for any recount or audit.

The Election Assistance Commission would conduct random, unannounced hand counts of the paper records in at least 2% of precincts in each state after every federal general election, starting with the November 2006 elections, and could expand the audit if it found cause for concern.

Voting machines could contain no undisclosed software — manufacturers must disclose source code to the Commission for public inspection — and no wireless, power-line, or concealed communication devices, and no component where votes are cast could be connected to the internet.

Testing laboratories could not be accredited if they had a financial interest in voting system manufacturers, and manufacturers would face conflict-of-interest standards barring partisan positions or campaign roles.
A person aggrieved by a violation of federal election requirements could file a complaint with the Attorney General, who must respond, and could also sue in court to enforce the requirements.

States would receive $150 million in additional federal funds to cover the new requirements, and voters with disabilities would get accessible verification mechanisms developed through a required federal study of best practices.

analysis.who_pays: Voting machine manufacturers would bear the cost of retrofitting or replacing paperless machines, publishing source code, and removing wireless and internet connections. State and local election officials would pay to implement the paper trail, preserve the records, and coordinate federal audits, offset in part by $150 million in authorized federal funds.
analysis.who_pays_short: Voting machine vendors and state election officials

drawbacks.text: Retrofitting paperless electronic machines with printers or replacing them entirely costs money, and the $150 million authorized in the bill may not fully cover state and local governments' implementation costs.

The federal hand-count audits require states to delay certifying election results until the audit is complete, which could slow official results, and the audits rely on the Election Assistance Commission having staff and funding to conduct unannounced counts nationwide.

Some machine vendors and election officials argued that adding printers to electronic machines introduces new failure points and that well-run elections do not need federally mandated audits — a real engineering and cost objection the bill's authors would have had to answer.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits were broad and durable: a paper trail for every voter and routine audits apply to every federal election and make recounts meaningful, which is the foundation for trusting close elections. The costs are real but modest relative to the stakes — election equipment is a small part of election budgets, and the bill included $150 million of federal money to offset the state burden. The bigger objection is practical, not philosophical: the audit machinery gives the Election Assistance Commission a large new operational role, and states would have to adapt quickly for the November 2006 elections.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Administration Committee the day it was introduced, gathered 222 cosponsors including 24 Republicans, but the committee never held a markup and the bill never reached the House floor before the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. Rush Holt of New Jersey introduced the Voter Confidence and Increased Accessibility Act of 2005 on February 2, 2005.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on House Administration the same day, where it stayed for the rest of the Congress.
It attracted 222 cosponsors — 197 Democrats, 24 Republicans, and 1 Independent — well over half the House.
The only further activity in the record was introductory remarks by the sponsor in July 2005 and April 2006; the committee held no markup and the House never voted on it.
The 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, and bills that never receive a vote expire and must be reintroduced from scratch.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Voting machine manufacturers kept selling closed, paperless electronic systems with no new federal requirements, and state and local election officials avoided the new paper-trail, audit, and software-disclosure mandates. Voters got no paper record and no federal audit requirement — Congress later addressed paper trails piecemeal through state laws rather than this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Voting machine vendors and unchanged state election practices

for.name: Rep. Rush Holt
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 2, 2005 and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor in July 2005 and April 2006.

against.name: Committee on House Administration
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and held no markup, hearing vote, or report on it for the entire 109th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — 222 cosponsors including 24 Republicans — but the committee that buried the bill was chaired by the House's majority party, and no vote was ever allowed on either side of the aisle.

industries.note: The bill would have forced vendors to retrofit paperless machines with voter-verifiable paper trails, disclose their source code for public inspection, remove wireless and internet connections, and prove no conflicts of interest. Vendors profited from closed, unauditable systems, so the bill's transparency requirements directly cut against their business model.

Election officials would have gained $150 million in federal funds but taken on new duties: preserving paper records, supporting federal hand-count audits, delaying certification until audits finish, and retraining staff.
Labs with financial ties to voting manufacturers would lose accreditation, and all labs would have to disclose their testing results to the Commission and the public.
